content:
While Apple is doing its best to protect former design chief Jony Ive from its lawsuit against OpenAI, the company may not be able to prevent the former design guru from being dragged into the case. Here's why.

OpenAI has the opportunity to put Apple in a very awkward position

In its lawsuit accusing OpenAI of misappropriating trade secrets, Apple has deliberately avoided mentioning Jony Ive. The hardware developed through Ive's company io Products in collaboration with OpenAI is at the very heart of Apple's allegations.

Apple at one point claimed in the lawsuit that "OpenAI and its co-conspirators have engaged in a pattern of organised infringement at the institutional level," which included io, but Apple only described it as "an enterprise co-founded by Mr Tang and other former Apple executives." Apart from Tang Tan and Chang Liu, who are directly accused of wrongdoing, the complaint makes no mention of Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executives by name.

Although it is still too early to say definitively whether Ive will be called to testify, it is certainly a possibility—especially if OpenAI decides to use him to embarrass or discomfort Apple.

This would put Apple in an exceptionally delicate position. Since leaving Apple in 2019, Ive has been publicly respectful toward the company in public appearances, which have typically been carefully orchestrated.

These have included attending events with Laurene Powell Jobs and ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive personally wrote a letter for the archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" project, recounting his experiences working with Jobs.

Apple, for its part, appears to have returned the courtesy, being notably restrained in its language when making adjustments to several of Ive's more controversial late-tenure decisions—including the MacBook's butterfly keyboard. Its deliberate effort to keep him at arm's length from the lawsuit is consistent with this approach.

But once the case enters the discovery phase, Apple will not have full control over who gets drawn in. Given that Ive is the founder of io Products and oversees the hardware project central to this dispute, OpenAI could argue that he has relevant knowledge about the product development process, the information the team relied upon, and whether Apple's trade secrets were involved.

Apple could then face the uncomfortable prospect of having to question Ive on the stand, challenge his testimony, or attempt to undermine the credibility of a former executive who shaped many of Apple's most iconic products.

This is not the first time Ive has been required to testify in litigation involving Apple. In 2012, he gave a deposition in Apple's patent lawsuit against Samsung, where he answered questions about Apple's design process and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

However, testifying for the opposing side could damage the relationship with Apple that he has carefully cultivated—and could even create friction with OpenAI, if Ive feels the company has unnecessarily dragged him into a dispute to pressure his former employer in negotiations.

Do you think Jony Ive will be pulled into this lawsuit? Let us know in the comments.
